summary: A first-person reflection on committing to a seasonal, local farm-to-table diet starting September 1, 2023. The author describes learning from local farmers and producers, taking part in community meals, and coming to see seasonal eating as a practice of sustainability, creativity, health and connection to nature's rhythms.
one_line: A personal narrative of eating only local, seasonal food from September 2023, covering farmer lessons, community, sustainability, health and creativity.
key_facts: The author began a seasonal, local diet on September 1, 2023, after a conversation with Michael Johnson.

Michael Johnson is a farmer at the Heartland Homestead who practices sustainable farming; he said, "Food doesn't just nourish the body. It's a story of the land, the climate, and the tender care of those who cultivate it."
On September 14 the author had a first fully local meal of roasted butternut squash with a kale and apple salad, all sourced from within twenty miles.
Beatrice Miller of Millstone Farm advocates organic methods and taught the author about crop rotation and enriching soil naturally.
Apples picked from Beatrice Miller's orchard on October 18 showed the farm's unique terroir, a term the author had reserved for wine.
On November 5 a community harvest dinner served only food grown, reared or produced within a fifty-mile radius, including heirloom tomato bruschetta and glazed heritage pork.
On November 12 Jason Rodriguez, who runs a small-scale permaculture operation, explained how permaculture designs sustainable, self-sufficient agricultural landscapes.
Choosing local ingredients became a gesture of reducing carbon footprint and supporting better farming techniques.
The author cites absence of preservatives and lower post-harvest nutrient degradation as physical benefits, and also gained mental tranquility.
Limited seasonal ingredients like a dozen parsnips, surplus beets and leafy greens after an October harvest spurred culinary creativity.
In winter, persimmons and Brussels sprouts led to heartier meals, and kale became sweeter with every frost.
The author concludes that seasonal eating gave structure to the year and a deeper connection between sustenance and the Earth.
